sections.md:
**Current phase:** FACT: BVS has completed two prototype trial series (dry bulk / terminal-stem in Q2 2024; LPG tankers / FCFS in Q3–Q4 2024). The project is in the prototype-to-commercialisation transition phase. *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

**Next phase — stated schedule:** FACT: "Prototype trials with the CBH Group and Marubeni Corporation have successfully concluded in the dry bulk and tanker segments, to be followed by more in 2025 with other consortium members and in other market segments." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

*Re-check window set:* Q2 2025 onwards — for new prototype trial results in additional market segments and/or commercial deployment announcement. The brief should be refreshed when those results are published.

**Multiple prototype versions confirmed:** FACT: "Multiple prototype versions are planned for development across various market segments with the participation of various stakeholders, with the aim of deploying the Blue Visby Solution as a neutral and independent platform designed to eliminate the most significant source of carbon inefficiency in the world seaborne trade." *Source: Marubeni press release, August 2023. https://www.marubeni.com/en/news/2023/release/00082.html

**Conversion triggers — from signal to operational or contractual pressure:**

*Analytical inference:* Three triggers would convert BVS from a monitored innovation to active commercial and compliance pressure:

1. **Regulatory recognition:** IMO CII rating methodology currently rewards speed reduction. If BVS-verified voyage data is accepted as CII performance evidence — or if FuelEU Maritime or EU ETS documentation frameworks reference arrival-time optimisation as a qualifying measure — adoption pressure on charterers and operators accelerates sharply. Bureau Veritas's methodology validation (May 2025) is a direct step toward this trigger.

2. **Critical mass of consortium members:** The SFTW problem cannot be solved bilaterally. *Analytical inference:* The academic research corroborating this brief (arXiv, 2025) models that information sharing in FCFS port queues produces measurable emissions reductions only when participating vessel share is sufficient — meaning conversion from pilot to systemic effect depends on a threshold proportion of fleet participation, not just individual vessel adoption.

3. **Commercial adoption clauses:** When major charterers or commodity traders begin inserting BVS participation clauses into voyage charter parties (analogous to how slow-steaming clauses entered standard contracts post-2008), the tool shifts from voluntary efficiency instrument to contractual compliance requirement.

**Regulatory connection — no-vacuum linkage:**
FACT: The BVS website states: "The reduction of operational emissions today is necessary pursuant to the IMO regulatory requirements of the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII), as well as the commitments of charterers, traders and cargo owners under SCOPE 3." *Source: Blue Visby Solution website. https://bluevisby.com/

*Analytical inference:* For cargo principals and traders operating under Scope 3 reporting frameworks (including CSRD and ISSB S2 alignment), BVS participation by their contracted carriers represents a verifiable, auditable emissions reduction in transport Scope 3 categories — a form of emissions performance that does not depend on fuel switching, capital expenditure, or retrofitting.

---

**Action 1 — Map contracted ocean carriers against BVS consortium membership.**
*Operational implication:* The workspace, in its role as ocean freight buyer or forwarder arranging ocean services on behalf of cargo-owner clients, should identify which of its contracted ocean carriers are among the 40+ BVS consortium members. This is a data-collection action, not a commercial commitment. It creates the foundation for Scope 3 reporting differentiation.

**Action 2 — Add BVS participation as a scored criterion in ocean carrier RFQ/RFP processes.**
*Analytical inference:* As the BVS moves toward commercialisation (stated 2025 further trials; Bureau Veritas validation complete), including BVS participation as a weighted sustainability criterion in ocean carrier procurement positions the workspace ahead of clients who will begin requiring verified Scope 3 transport reductions under CSRD and investor frameworks. The action costs nothing now and creates leverage at contract renewal.

**Action 3 — Request voyage-level emissions reporting terms from BVS-participating carriers.**
*Analytical inference:* The Bureau Veritas validation process is building toward "transparent, verifiable data supporting the system's impact" being available per voyage. Workspaces that establish data-sharing expectations with carriers now — before commercial deployment formalises reporting formats — will be better positioned to feed BVS-verified data into Scope 3 disclosures when the methodology is formally integrated into MRV frameworks.

**Action 4 — Brief sustainability and commercial teams on the FCFS trial result before Q2 2025 results arrive.**
*Analytical inference:* The next prototype cohort is stated for 2025 in additional market segments. When those results are published, clients with ocean-freight Scope 3 commitments will ask about them. Teams that have already understood the two-environment trial results (terminal-stem vs FCFS) can give informed answers; teams briefed only after publication are reactive.

**Action 5 — Flag charter party speed terms for legal review.**
*Legal Confirmation Required:* Standard voyage charter party speed and performance warranty clauses may conflict with BVS speed-reduction recommendations. Whether a carrier's BVS participation constitutes a deviation or performance breach under the workspace's existing freight contracts requires maritime law counsel review before the workspace recommends or relies on BVS participation by its contracted carriers.

**Monitor trigger:** Re-check this brief when 2025 prototype trial results in new segments are published, or when IMO or EU Commission issues guidance on whether arrival-time optimisation data qualifies for CII or EU ETS MRV purposes.

---

**Consortium coordinator and technology provider:**
FACT: The Blue Visby Consortium is co-ordinated by Helsinki-based software company NAPA Oy and London-based law firm Stephenson Harwood. *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

FACT: Blue Visby Services Ltd. is established at Minster House, 42 Mincing Lane, London EC3R 7AE; established July 2021; representatives Pekka Pakkanen and Christian Wounlund; main business is software service development for ship operation. *Source: Marubeni Corporation press release, 8 August 2023. https://www.marubeni.com/en/news/2023/release/00082.html

**Verified consortium members participating in trials:**
- FACT: Marubeni Corporation — charter operator of the 16 LPG tankers in the second prototype trial, and earlier gas and chemical tanker fleet used in verification simulations. *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024; Marubeni press release, August 2023. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/ and https://www.marubeni.com/en/news/2023/release/00082.html
- FACT: CBH Group — terminal operator whose terminal stem environment was the basis for the first (Q2 2024) prototype trial involving Supramax bulkers. Kwinana, Western Australia terminal named. *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024; Bureau Veritas press release, May 2025. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

**Independent methodology validator:**
FACT: Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore conducted an independent technical review of the BVS emissions reduction methodology in May 2025. "This involved assessing the robustness of the approach used to quantify savings by comparing actual voyage data – including AIS-derived routes and speed profiles – with optimized scenarios generated by the Blue Visby Solution algorithm." The assessment also covered "the practicability of the methodology in relation to data acquisition and reliability, the completeness of the methodology by reference to all significant factors and also the neutrality of outcome, by reference to the financial interests of the parties concerned." *Source: Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore, May 2025. https://marine-offshore.bureauveritas.com/newsroom/bureau-veritas-validates-methodology-used-blue-visby-solution-estimate-its-effect-shipping

**What the parties want:** *Analytical inference:* Shipowners and charterers face structurally opposed incentives under standard maritime contracts — charterers bear fuel cost while shipowners control speed decisions. The BVS benefit-sharing mechanism (modelled on the maritime general average tradition) is designed to resolve this split by distributing fuel savings across both parties, making speed reduction commercially rational for both sides. The involvement of NAPA Oy (voyage optimisation software), Stephenson Harwood (maritime law), and a classification society validator (Bureau Veritas) suggests the consortium is building the institutional and legal infrastructure needed for scalable adoption, not merely technical proof.

**Stated membership scale:** FACT: "Over a period of several years, Blue Visby Solution has progressed through a series of stages—including multiple proof of concept studies and pilot programs—while the Blue Visby Consortium has grown to comprise over 25 member organizations, including Marubeni, over a period of less than 12 months." *Source: Marubeni Corporation press release, August 2023. https://www.marubeni.com/en/news/2023/release/00082.html

FACT: Offshore Energy (November 2024) references "40+ members of the Blue Visby Consortium." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

*Analytical inference:* The growth from 25+ to 40+ consortium members over the observed period indicates accelerating industry engagement, consistent with the regulatory pressure timeline created by IMO CII and EU ETS.

---

**For workspaces acting as ocean freight buyers or Scope 3 reporting entities:**

*Analytical inference:* Cargo principals and freight buyers who specify BVS-participating carriers in their tendering can credibly claim verified, third-party-validated GHG reductions on ocean legs without fuel surcharge uplift, new vessel requirements, or SAF procurement. This is a near-term differentiation, not a 2030 ambition.

*Analytical inference:* Freight forwarders who integrate BVS carrier participation into their sustainability reporting to clients — particularly clients with CSRD or investor-facing Scope 3 commitments — gain a credible, auditable emissions-reduction narrative on ocean legs that competitors without access to BVS-participating carrier pools cannot replicate.

**Bureau Veritas validation as competitive signal:**

FACT: BV's independent validation confirmed "the simulations accurately reflect real-world voyage behaviors and optimization effects, supporting the credibility of projected emission avoidance." BV further stated it is "helping pave the way for innovative digital practices to be integrated into mainstream compliance and emissions reporting." *Source: Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore, May 2025. https://marine-offshore.bureauveritas.com/newsroom/bureau-veritas-validates-methodology-used-blue-visby-solution-estimate-its-effect-shipping

*Industry interpretation:* Bureau Veritas validation by a Tier-1 classification society is the credential that enables BVS emissions reductions to enter compliance and MRV reporting frameworks. Competing operational optimisation tools that lack equivalent independent methodology validation are in a weaker position as IMO and EU regulators tighten emissions evidence standards.

**Named competitors and their positions:**
No sourced reporting on named competing arrival-time optimisation products and their comparative validation status was identified in the available source pool. This is an explicit research gap.

*Analytical inference:* The BVS's multilateral architecture (40+ consortium members, benefit-sharing mechanism, classification society validation, legal firm co-ordination) creates a structural moat that bilateral "virtual arrival" agreements — which BVS explicitly distinguishes itself from — do not replicate. FACT: "This multilateral feature differentiates the Blue Visby Solution from earlier attempts at a 'Virtual Arrival' approach, which were bilateral between shipowners and charterers." *Source: Blue Visby Solution website. https://bluevisby.com/

---

MONITORING

The Blue Visby Solution (BVS) has completed its second series of prototype trials — the BVS/Marubeni Prototype Trial (PT) — involving LPG tankers operating in a First Come First Served (FCFS) port environment. *Source: "New Blue Visby prototype trials project average GHG savings of 29%," Offshore Energy, 11 November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

FACT: "The Blue Visby Solution project (BVS) recently completed a series of prototype trials, involving 16 LPG tankers under charter by Marubeni Corporation, a Blue Visby Consortium member, across 40 voyages during a period of three months." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

FACT: "Approximately 31 actionable recommendations for vessels to reduce speed were issued, with projected fuel and GHG savings of about 29%, on average. This average figure was confirmed in the results from the vessels that followed the BVS recommendations." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

FACT: "These savings were delivered through speed reductions from an average speed of 13.6 knots, down to an average speed of 10.6 knots." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

This second trial follows the first series completed in Q2 2024. FACT: "The BVS/Marubeni PT follows on from the prototype trials that were completed in Q2 2024 involving Supramax bulkers under charter by Blue Visby Consortium member CBH Group, which demonstrated fuel and GHG emissions savings of approximately 8-28%." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

The two trials together cover the two principal operating environments in maritime trade. FACT: "The combined experience of two sets of prototype trials over a period of six months, with the invaluable support of Blue Visby Consortium members CBH Group and Marubeni Corporation, has demonstrated the feasibility of deploying the Blue Visby Solution in the two main operating environments in maritime trade: terminal stem and First Come First Served." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024 (quoting BVS Coordinators Haris Zografakis and Pekka Pakkanen). https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

**What triggered the trials:** The BVS has developed iteratively over several years. FACT: "Over a period of several years, and with support from 40+ members of the Blue Visby Consortium, which is co-ordinated by Helsinki-based software company NAPA Oy and London-based law firm Stephenson Harwood, the project has progressed iteratively through several stages: from academic studies to proofs of concept, to hindcast simulations in real operating conditions, to virtual pilots with the use of digital twins and, finally, to prototype trials." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

**The underlying inefficiency being targeted:** FACT: "Ever since the Age of Sail, cargo ships have followed the same operational practice: 'Sail Fast, Then Wait' (SFTW). Ships sail to their destination at their service speed, without regard for the local conditions, and there wait at the anchorage until a berth becomes available. This practice accounts for about 15% or the total marine fuel consumption and is incentivised commercially and contractually." *Source: Blue Visby Solution website. https://bluevisby.com/

FACT: "About 7% of the entire life of a tanker or a bulk carrier is spent waiting at anchorage." *Source: Blue Visby Solution website. https://bluevisby.com/

**Regulatory backdrop activating urgency:** FACT: Bureau Veritas confirmed in its May 2025 methodology validation that "the shipping industry enters a new regulatory era – with the EU ETS expanding and IMO regulations tightening – the Blue Visby Solution represents a pragmatic and forward-looking tool." *Source: "Bureau Veritas Validates the methodology used by the Blue Visby Solution to estimate its effect on Shipping Emissions," Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore, 22 May 2025. https://marine-offshore.bureauveritas.com/newsroom/bureau-veritas-validates-methodology-used-blue-visby-solution-estimate-its-effect-shipping

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- Two verified prototype trial series have now been completed: dry bulk / terminal-stem (Q2 2024, 8–28% GHG savings) and LPG tankers / FCFS (Q3–Q4 2024, ~29% average GHG savings). Both are sourced from consortium reporting.
- Bureau Veritas, a Tier-1 classification society, independently validated the BVS emissions reduction methodology in May 2025, confirming robustness of AIS-derived voyage data comparison and digital twin simulation.
- The solution requires no new vessel hardware, no alternative fuels, and no capital expenditure. It works on the existing fleet through optimised arrival timing.
- The system has been demonstrated in both operating environments used in maritime trade: terminal-stem (fixed berth allocation) and First Come First Served (open queue).

**Questions to pose to clients:**
- Do your voyage charter party terms currently allow or restrict speed variation on ocean legs? A standard charter may contain speed and performance warranties that need review before BVS participation is contractually possible.
- Are your contracted ocean carriers consortium members? If not, which segments of your fleet are unaddressed?
- How are you currently accounting for ocean-leg Scope 3 emissions in your sustainability disclosures? Is there an auditable evidence trail from your carriers?

**Claims to avoid / pitfalls:**
- Do not assert that 29% GHG savings apply universally. The 29% figure is specific to the FCFS LPG tanker trial; the terminal-stem trial produced 8–28%. Route, segment, port congestion, and participating-vessel proportion all affect the outcome. Overstating the figure in a client meeting exposes the workspace to credibility risk if the carrier's actual performance differs.
- Do not assert that BVS is a compliant IMO CII or EU ETS reporting instrument without legal confirmation. Bureau Veritas validated the methodology, but regulatory acceptance of BVS data for CII rating or EU ETS MRV purposes is not confirmed in any of the available sources. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether BVS-verified voyage emissions reductions are accepted by flag state administrations for CII rating calculation, or by the EU MRV system for EU ETS compliance, requires counsel and regulator confirmation.
- Do not describe BVS as commercially deployed at scale. The project is at prototype trial stage, with further trials planned for 2025. Commercial deployment terms, pricing, and availability are not publicly documented in the available sources.

---

**Filtered to the workspace's ocean-mode operations and cargo principals / freight forwarder roles:**

*Operational implication:* For workspaces whose clients are commodity traders, bulk cargo principals, or LPG/chemical charterers, BVS participation by contracted ocean carriers becomes a Scope 3 emissions reporting lever. The mechanism is: contracted carriers reduce ocean passage speed by approximately 3 knots (13.6 → 10.6 knots demonstrated in the second trial); fuel consumption falls; verified GHG savings of ~29% (FCFS environment) or ~8–28% (terminal-stem environment) are attributed to the voyage; the reduction flows into the cargo owner's Scope 3 Category 4 (upstream transportation) account.

*Operational implication:* No capital expenditure is involved on the cargo owner's side. FACT: "All these benefits can be achieved with existing technologies... but requires no new on-board systems or retrofits." *Source: Blue Visby Solution website. https://bluevisby.com/ The only operational change for cargo principals is contractual: ensuring voyage charter parties permit or require BVS participation.

**Transit time implications — the commercial trade-off:**

*Analytical inference:* Speed reduction from 13.6 to 10.6 knots on a 10-day voyage extends passage time by approximately 2.7 days before anchorage waiting time is subtracted. If anchorage waiting time averages several days (consistent with 7% of vessel lifetime at anchorage cited by BVS), total port-to-port time may be neutral or slightly extended depending on port congestion. For cargo verticals where transit time is commercially critical — including temperature-controlled bulk, time-sensitive chemical cargoes, and LPG — the net transit time impact is a parameter that cargo owners should request from carriers on a route-specific basis. FACT: "effect on transit time for specific cargo verticals and routes requires carrier-specific data and is not quantified in the available source material."

**Monitoring scale in FCFS environment — operational complexity signal:**

FACT: "A key parameter of the BVS/Marubeni PT involved monitoring the operational status of a total of some 919 vessels on a 24/7 basis to ensure that the vessels participating in the PT would not be overtaken by non-participating vessels." *Source: Offshore Energy, November 2024. https://www.offshore-energy.biz/new-blue-visby-prototype-trials-project-average-ghg-savings-of-29/

*Analytical inference:* The 919-vessel monitoring requirement illustrates that BVS's FCFS functionality requires significant real-time fleet surveillance infrastructure — not just bilateral communication between operator and vessel. This is a platform-level service, not a charterer-side tool; cargo principals and forwarders consume the output (arrival time recommendation), not the infrastructure.

**Cost impact on freight rates:**
*Specific cost-impact figure (fuel savings value per voyage, freight rate adjustment, or pass-through mechanism) not available from primary sources at the time of this authoring pass.* The BVS includes a cost-and-benefit sharing mechanism (Blue GA), but the commercial terms under which savings are distributed between shipowner and charterer are not publicly quantified in the available sources.

---

Blue Visby Solution ™ Multilateral across the supply chain Deploying a a sharing mechanism to remove split incentives Applicable to the existing fleet, as well as the future fleet powered by carbon-neutral fuels Complementary to individual vessels’ voyage planning Supporting any individual port’s just-in-time projects Adapting existing maritime norms and contractual structures Collaborative. Transparent,  Neutral,  Independent Ever since the Age of Sail, cargo ships have followed the same operational practice: “Sail Fast, Then Wait” (SFTW). Ships sail to their destination at their service speed, without regard for the local conditions, and there wait at the anchorage until a berth becomes available. This practice accounts for about 15% or the total marine fuel consumption and is incentivised commercially and contractually. The Blue Visby Solution has devised both the technology and the methodology for sharing the financial benefits of reduced fuel consumption, so that both shipowners and charterers benefit financially. Eradicating SFTW will reduce the carbon footprint of the maritime industry by about 15% or about 45 million tonnes of CO2 across the tanker fleet and bulker fleets. These reductions in emissions are available today, The Blue Visby Solution delivers emissions reductions of about 15% through a speed reduction of about 1 knot on average, which is well within the operational parameters of the existing commercial fleet. The reduction of operational emissions today is necessary pursuant to the IMO regulatory requirements of the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII),  as well as the commitments of charterers, traders and cargo owners under SCOPE 3. Reducing emissions today is also imperative to reduce committed and cumulative emissions and meet the 1.5C target. from the world’s current fleet. But these savings will also be necessary tomorrow, as adopting zero-carbon fuels While the decarbonization destination is set, both the target dates and the paths differ. Amidst all that uncertainty, one thing is certain: All potential replacements for marine fossil fuels – including ammonia, methanol, and hydrogen – have a lower energy density, and are far more expensive than marine fuel oil. Their adoption will require a step-change in operational efficiency, and SFTW is simply unsustainable on the path to decarbonization. About 7% of the entire life of a tanker or a bulk carrier is spent waiting at anchorage. It is estimated that trillions of USD will be required for the maritime industry to decarbonize. It is inconceivable that this level of investment will be made for all those new ships burning expensive new fuels to Sail Fast, Then Wait. will be impossible without removing the unsustainable operational inefficiency of SFTW. These savings are in addition to any available reductions gained through voyage optimization of individual ships The Blue Visby Solution does not seek to optimize the voyage of an individual ship, but only to optimize the arrival time of a group of ships sailing to the same destination. and to any retrofit of other efficiency solutions. GHG emissions reduction is not the only benefit of the Blue Visby Solution. It also reduces underwater noise pollution and whale strike risk; According to independent research, adoption of Blue Visby Solution would reduce underwater noise pollution by 45% and the risk of striking whales by 40%. it improves the air quality outside ports; it reduces the risk of collisions and anchor loss at busy anchorages, and it reduces hull fouling, According to several publications, biofouling increases significantly every day of anchorage in warm waters, and hull fouling contributes greatly to increased fuel consumption and GHG emissions. which in turn improves vessels’ operational efficiency. All these benefits can be achieved with existing technologies The Blue Visby Solution deploys state-of-the-art systems – optimization software, technologies for weather and maritime conditions monitoring and forecasting, earth observation systems, and electronic charts – but requires no new on-board systems or retrofits. and within the existing regulatory framework, The Blue Visby Solution is based on a contractual architecture that is designed to be compatible with the standard terms of maritime contracts, and does not require new legislation or regulations. The Blue Visby Solution leverages one of the most enduring features of the world of maritime trade: Party autonomy and freedom of contract under English law. applying a systemic The Blue Visby Solution adopts a systems optimization approach and does not seek to optimize the operations of an individual ship or an individual port. Instead, it approaches a group of vessels steaming to the same destination as a system and applies Theory of Constraint optimization principles to optimize their arrival, to minimize their emissions. approach that goes beyond an individual ship The Blue Visby Solution is compatible with all voyage planning and weather routing software. Not only does it not compete with the providers of such software, but it assists their task by providing a target arrival date for individual ships. or an individual contract. The Blue Visby Solution includes a multilateral sharing mechanism for the costs and benefits of its implementation amongst all stakeholders of the vessel’s voyage. This multilateral feature differentiates the Blue Visby Solution from earlier attempts at a “Virtual Arrival” approach, which were bilateral between shipowners and charterers. Blue Visby™ has a sole purpose: to make shipping more sustainable by eradicating Sail Fast, Then Wait. The Blue Visby Solution combines technology with long-established maritime traditions of cost-sharing, The main obstacle to removing operational inefficiencies is the so-called problem of split incentives. The Blue Visby Solution removes that obstacle by introducing a sharing mechanism for the costs and benefits of its implementation: Blue GA. Its inspiration is the age-old maritime tradition of general average, under which the stakeholders of the vessel’s voyage contribute towards the expenses necessary to “save the common maritime adventure”, when it is threatened by an emergency or by the perils of the seas. The climate emergency is also a threat, not to the common maritime adventure of one ship, but to the entire world of maritime trade. The Blue Visby Solution “declares general average” to remove the obstacle of split incentives. collaboration and mutuality. The maritime industry is often criticized as being individualistic and hyper-competitive. However, it is also profoundly collaborative when dealing with common threats. At the voyage level, the best illustration is the general average. More widely, collaboration is exemplified by industry associations, which set common standards and deal with problems that are common to all. An integral part of the Blue Visby Solution is an mutual association modelled on P&I Clubs, which oversee the relationship between the participants and administers Blue GA. The Blue Visby Solution deploys the maritime industry’s own DNA and introduces the values of neutrality, independence and integrity, The Blue Visby Solution proudly builds on the maritime industry’s unique strengths, history and traditions. It is committed to remaining neutral, independent, inclusive and transparent to reduce emissions to benefit the entire industry. to enable a new and environmentally better way of doing things. In his book The Climate Emergency, Bill Gates writes that “innovation is not only new devices and new technologies, but also new ways of doing things”. The Blue Visby Solution has created a new way of doing things, enabling international maritime trade to deliver CO 2 emissions reductions at an unprecedented scale in this hard-to-abate industry. Blue Visby Solution™ Supports the UN's Sustainable Development Goals © Blue Visby Services Ltd. The Blue Visby Solution is protected by patents and trademarks Manage consent

Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore (BV), a global leader in testing, inspection, and certification, has confirmed the validity of the emissions reduction methodology of the Blue Visby Solution , a multilateral platform developed by the Blue Visby Consortium, which aims to cut emissions from shipping by around 15% through coordinated, sector-wide behavioral change. The Blue Visby Solution tackles one of the industry’s most persistent carbon inefficiencies – the practice of “sail fast then wait,” – where ships rush to port only to spend hours or days idling at anchorage. Instead, participating vessels receive optimized arrival times calculated by the Blue Visby Solution algorithm, enabling them to slow steam, reduce fuel consumption, and minimize congestion. This approach does not rely on new fuels or hardware, but rather on a systemic optimization of the ocean passage, contractual refinements and a methodology for sharing the financial consequences, making it an actionable decarbonization strategy that is available today. In support of the development of the Blue Visby Solution, BV has conducted an independent technical review of the Blue Visby methodology used to estimate its effect on fuel and emissions. This involved assessing the robustness of the approach used to quantify savings by comparing actual voyage data – including AIS-derived routes and speed profiles – with optimized scenarios generated by the Blue Visby Solution algorithm. In addition, BV assessed the practicability of the methodology in relation to data acquisition and reliability, the completeness of the methodology by reference to all significant factors and also the neutrality of outcome, by reference to the financial interests of the parties concerned.  BV also evaluated the reliability of the digital twin simulations underpinning Blue Visby’s modelling framework. The assessment confirmed that the simulations accurately reflect real-world voyage behaviors and optimization effects, supporting the credibility of projected emission avoidance. Through this work, BV is helping ensure the solution is technically sound and verifiable for regulators, shipowners, charterers, and other industry stakeholders. As part of the ongoing work, the Blue Visby Solution team and BV will continue to analyze simulation results, validate assumptions, and jointly consolidate findings based on a representative sample of anonymized voyages, employing arrival time optimization as a practical and impactful decarbonization strategy. This process aims to provide the industry with transparent, verifiable data supporting the system’s impact. By validating the methodology and confirming the robustness of the simulations, BV is helping pave the way for innovative digital practices to be integrated into mainstream compliance and emissions reporting. As the shipping industry enters a new regulatory era – with the EU ETS expanding and IMO regulations tightening – the Blue Visby Solution represents a pragmatic and forward-looking tool. By reducing fuel use and emissions through better timing, the platform helps shipowners and charterers align commercial performance with environmental responsibility. Image Matthieu de Tugny President Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore The Blue Visby Solution combines technology with long-established maritime traditions of cost-sharing, collaboration and mutuality. The collaboration illustrates how industry-wide coordination can unlock efficiencies that benefit all stakeholders. We are proud to contribute our expertise to initiatives that make the decarbonization of shipping both credible and achievable. Haris Zografakis, Blue Visby Consortium co-ordinator, said: "Key to the Blue Visby Solution is its neutrality and the integrity in estimating avoided emissions. The technical evaluation and validation from Bureau Veritas is a testament to the hard work and dedication of the teams at Bureau Veritas and Blue Visby and the support of the Blue Visby Consortium.”  Photo caption: Representatives of Blue Visby and CBH Inc. presenting the Master of the M/V Sifnos with a commemorative certificate of his ship's Blue Visby voyage to CBH's terminal at Kwinana, Western Australia. Prototype to Reduce CO2 Emissions in the Global Maritime Trade Aug. 08, 2023 Marubeni Corporation Marubeni Corporation (hereinafter, “Marubeni”) participated in the Blue Visby Consortium in August of last year to develop an integrated system, Blue Visby Solution (hereinafter, the “System”), which notifies ships of the optimal date and time to make arrival at their destination. The Blue Visby Consortium conducted verification towards implementation of the System using a fleet of gas and chemical tankers operated by Marubeni. It was confirmed through this verification that CO2 emissions could be reduced by an average of approximately 15% over a total of 625 voyages of 68 vessels operated and chartered by Marubeni. Marubeni and Blue Visby Services Ltd. (hereinafter, “Blue Visby”) have since signed a Letter of Intent for the development of a prototype version of Blue Visby Solution (hereinafter, “Blue Visby Prototype/Chemicals”). Ships waiting to enter their destination port Solution simulation results, with circle size indicating the relative amount of potential CO2 emission reduction Blue Visby Solution comprises software, an operational system, and contractual architecture, aimed at improving inefficient fuel consumption due to the practice of cargo ships that Sail Fast Then Wait near their destination, and thereby deliver very substantial reductions in GHG emissions. Over a period of several years, Blue Visby Solution has progressed through a series of stages–including multiple proof of concept studies and pilot programs–while the Blue Visby Consortium has grown to comprise over 25 member organizations, including Marubeni,  over a period of less than 12 months. Blue Visby Prototype/Chemicals, which the consortium is currently planning to develop, will be a pioneering basic model. Multiple prototype versions are planned for development across various market segments with the participation of various stakeholders, with the aim of deploying the Blue Visby Solution as a neutral and independent platform designed to eliminate the most significant source of carbon inefficiency in the world seaborne trade.  Company Overview Name: Blue Visby Services Ltd. New Blue Visby prototype trials project average GHG savings of 29% - Offshore Energy Direct naar inhoud Offshore-Energy.biz offshoreWIND.biz DredgingToday.com NavalToday.com Exhibition and Conference Advertising , go to home Green Marine Hydrogen Marine Energy Subsea Fossil Energy Alternative Fuels More News Search Menu Green Marine Sub menu Alternative renewables Energy Efficiency & Innovation Ports & Infrastructure Propulsion Shipbuilding Regulations & Policy Hydrogen Sub menu Production Transport & Storage Technology & Innovation Valleys, Hubs & Corridors Funding & Regulation Marine Energy Sub menu Tidal & Wave Energy Floating Solar OTEC Alternative Markets Policy & Funding Subsea Sub menu Interconnectors Cabling Vehicles Interventions & Surveys Pipes Production & Processing Fossil Energy Sub menu Oil & Gas Rigs FPSO Decommissioning Low-Carbon Transition Offshore wind Sub menu Foundations Grid Turbines Vessels Wind Farms Dredging Sub menu Dredgers Efficiency Infrastructure Exhibition & Conference Sub menu About OEEC Become Exhibitor Partners Previous edition Media Center Advertising Events Newsletter Jobs News Report your news Companies About us Contact Back to overview Home Energy Efficiency & Innovation New Blue Visby prototype trials project average GHG savings of 29% New Blue Visby prototype trials project average GHG savings of 29% IT & Software November 11, 2024, by Naida Hakirevic Prevljak The second prototype trials of the Blue Visby software involving liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tankers have demonstrated that the solution can support various segments of the maritime industry and adapt to different scenarios while achieving substantial fuel and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions savings. Courtesy of Blue Visby Consortium The Blue Visby Solution project (BVS) recently completed a series of prototype trials, involving 16 LPG tankers under charter by Marubeni Corporation, a Blue Visby Consortium member, across 40 voyages during a period of three months. The BVS/Marubeni PT was designed to test the BVS technology acting as a decision-support tool in a “First Come First Served” (FCFS) operational environment. For the purposes of this trial, BVS technology provided the necessary optimization information and recommendations for the operator to decide whether or not to implement BVS, to reduce GHG emissions by mitigating the effects of “ Sail Fast Then Wait “ (SFTW). Due to the FCFS operational environment, a key parameter of the BVS/Marubeni PT involved monitoring the operational status of a total of some 919 vessels on a 24/7 basis to ensure that the vessels participating in the PT would not be overtaken by non-participating vessels. Approximately 31 actionable recommendations for vessels to reduce speed were issued, with projected fuel and GHG savings of about 29% , on average. This average figure was confirmed in the results from the vessels that followed the BVS recommendations. These savings were delivered through speed reductions from an average speed of 13.6 knots, down to an average speed of 10.6 knots. According to the consortium partners, the BVS/Marubeni PT demonstrated: substantial GHG emissions savings; the value of BVS as a decision-support tool, including in cases where a commercial decision is taken not to reduce speed, or to reduce speed only for part of a voyage. The feasibility of individual ships using BVS to reduce GHG emissions in a FCFS environment, without suffering any commercial disadvantage, even in the absence of wider co-ordination or terminal involvement. The BVS/Marubeni PT follows on from the prototype trials that were completed in Q2 2024 involving Supramax bulkers under charter by Blue Visby Consortium member CBH Group, which demonstrated fuel and GHG emissions savings of approximately 8-28%. Related Article Maiden Blue Visby trial shows promising shipping emissions reduction IT & Software The BVS/CBH Group prototype trial was designed to test the BVS in the context of optimizing for the needs of a terminal stem, rather than in an FCFS environment, which was the case in the BVS/Marubeni PT. “Over a period of several years, the Blue Visby Solution project has progressed iteratively through studies, simulations, virtual pilots to prototype trials. The combined experience of two sets of prototype trials over a period of six months, with the invaluable support of Blue Visby Consortium members CBH Group and Marubeni Corporation, has demonstrated the feasibility of deploying the Blue Visby Solution in the two main operating environments in maritime trade: terminal stem and First Come First Served,” Haris Zografakis and Pekka Pakkanen, Coordinators of the Blue Visby Consortium, commented. “During this Prototype Trial, we successfully demonstrated the capabilities of the technical system in challenging First Come First Served operational environments. The groundbreaking work of our research team during the past year has enabled us to use a wide range of new data and optimisation constraints, allowing us to solve some of the optimization challenges present in a competitive operational environment with a limited number of participating ships. The experience and the outcome of this Prototype Trial demonstrate that the Blue Visby Solution can adapt to different operational needs and use cases, supporting various segments of the industry ,” Kimmo Laaksonen , Chief Technology Officer of Blue Visby, explained. ‘Sail Fast Then Wait’ The Blue Visby Solution is an integrated system that notifies ships of the optimal date and time for arriving at their destination, eradicating the industry practice of “Sail Fast, Then Wait” . According to the consortium, the SFTW practice can be justified for various reasons, but it is responsible for about 20% of shipping’s carbon footprint . SFTW cannot be eradicated through the actions of individual ships, or bilaterally as between an individual shipowner and an individual charterer. It is “a systemic challenge that requires a systemic solution”, the Blue Visby Consortium claims. Specifically, the solution combines software, operations, and contracts to systemically optimize the ocean passage of participating ships and thereby reduce GHG emissions. It does not interfere with the voyage planning or weather routing of individual ships, and it does not interfere with berthing or port operations. A crucial component of the multilateral nature of the Blue Visby Solution is a benefit-sharing mechanism, which incentivizes participation and removes the obstacle of split incentives. Over a period of several years, and with support from 40+ members of the Blue Visby Consortium, which is co-ordinated by Helsinki-based software company NAPA Oy and London-based law firm Stephenson Harwood, the project has progressed iteratively through several stages: from academic studies to proofs of concept, to hindcast simulations in real operating conditions, to virtual pilots with the use of digital twins and, finally, to prototype trials. Prototype trials with the CBH Group and Marubeni Corporation have successfully concluded in the dry bulk and tanker segments, to be followed by more in 2025 with other consortium members and in other market segments. **Article 1 (the finding).** "The unit rates for charging zones for 2015 set out in the Annex are in compliance with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013."

**Article 2 (addressees).** "This Decision is addressed to the Republic of Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, the Kingdom of Denmark, the Republic of Estonia, Ireland, the Hellenic Republic, the Kingdom of Spain, the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Cyprus, the Republic of Latvia, the Republic of Lithuania, Hungary, the Republic of Malta, the Republic of Poland, the Portuguese Republic, Romania, the Republic of Slovenia, the Republic of Finland, the Kingdom of Sweden and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland."

**Recalculation clause (recital 8).** Because final second-reference-period performance plans were not adopted before 1 November 2014, Member States are to recalculate their 2015 unit rates where necessary once final plans are adopted, apply the recalculated rates as early as possible during 2015, and carry any resulting difference into the 2016 unit-rate calculation.

[penalty_summary] No penalty: the source text contains no penalty, fine, or enforcement provision; this Decision is a compliance-confirmation instrument, not an enforcement action, and sets no sanction for airline or freight operators at the time of this authoring pass.

*Operational implication:* This Decision confirms specific 2015 unit-rate submissions from 20 Member States as compliant; it does not itself set or change any unit rate, and does not apply to Member States outside the Article 2 addressee list. Given that final performance plans were not adopted before 1 November 2014, the Decision also contemplates a later recalculation of the 2015 rates, with any difference carried into the 2016 calculation, so the rates confirmed here may not be the final rates actually applied.

**Open question:** the source capture does not include the Annex referenced in Article 1 (the specific numeric unit rates by charging zone); the actual figures were not found in this capture.

This brief covers Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2015/670 of 27 April 2015 on the compliance of unit rates for charging zones for 2015 under Article 17 of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013 (notified under document C(2015) 2635) (Text with EEA relevance) (CELEX 32015D0670). It is adopted under "Having regard to Regulation (EC) No 550/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 March 2004 on the provision of air navigation services in the Single European Sky (the service provision Regulation)", and in particular Article 15(4) thereof.

It is dated "Done at Brussels, 27 April 2015."

Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013 sets a common EU charging scheme for air navigation services, tied to the performance scheme's cost-efficiency targets for the second reference period (2015-2019). Each year the Commission must assess Member States' proposed unit rates for their charging zones.

"Pursuant to Article 17(1)(b) and (c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, the Commission is to assess the unit rates for charging zones for 2015 submitted by the Member States to the Commission by 1 June 2014 following the requirements of Article 9(1) and 9(2) of that Regulation. That assessment concerns the compliance of those unit rates with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013."

Having carried out that assessment with the support of the Performance Review Body and Eurocontrol's Central Route Charges Office, the Commission found:

"On the basis of that assessment, the Commission has found, in accordance with Article 17(1)(d) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, that the unit rates for charging zones for 2015 submitted by the United Kingdom, Ireland, Bulgaria, Romania, Cyprus, Greece, Malta, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Slovenia, Hungary, Poland, Lithuania, Denmark, Sweden, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Portugal and Spain are in compliance with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013."

"Given that the final performance plans for the second reference period were not adopted before 1 November 2014, it is recalled that, in accordance with Article 17(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, the Member States are required to recalculate the unit rates for charging zones for 2015 where necessary on the basis of the final adopted performance plans and apply those recalculated rates as early as possible in the course of 2015 and to carry over any difference due to the temporary application of the unit rates set out in this Decision in the calculation of the unit rates for 2016."

         <p class="oj-doc-ti" id="d1e40-25-1">
            COMMISSION IMPLEMENTING DECISION (EU) 2015/670</p>
         <p class="oj-doc-ti">of 27 April 2015
         </p>
         <p class="oj-doc-ti">on the compliance of unit rates for charging zones for 2015 under Article 17 of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013</p>
         <p class="oj-doc-ti">
            <span class="oj-sp-normal">
               <span class="oj-italic">(notified under document C(2015) 2635)</span>
            </span>
         </p>
         <p class="oj-doc-ti">(Only the Bulgarian, Spanish, Czech, Danish, Estonian, Greek, English, Croatian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Hungarian, Maltese, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Slovenian, Finnish and Swedish texts are authentic)</p>
         <p class="oj-doc-ti">(Text with EEA relevance)</p>
      </div>
      <div class="eli-subdivision" id="pbl_1">
         <p class="oj-normal">THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION,</p>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="cit_1">
            <p class="oj-normal">Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union,</p>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="cit_2">
            <p class="oj-normal">Having regard to Regulation (EC) No 550/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 March 2004 on the provision of air navigation services in the Single European Sky (the service provision Regulation) <a id="ntc1-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0001" href="#ntr1-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0001">(<span class="oj-super oj-note-tag">1</span>)</a>, and in particular Article 15(4) thereof,</p>
         </div>
         <p class="oj-normal">Whereas:</p>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_1">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(1)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013 <a id="ntc2-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0002" href="#ntr2-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0002">(<span class="oj-super oj-note-tag">2</span>)</a> lays down a common charging scheme for air navigation services. The common charging scheme is an integral element in reaching the objectives of the performance scheme as established under Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 549/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council <a id="ntc3-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0003" href="#ntr3-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0003">(<span class="oj-super oj-note-tag">3</span>)</a> and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 390/2013 <a id="ntc4-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0004" href="#ntr4-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0004">(<span class="oj-super oj-note-tag">4</span>)</a>.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_2">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(2)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">Commission Implementing Decision 2014/132/EU <a id="ntc5-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0005" href="#ntr5-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0005">(<span class="oj-super oj-note-tag">5</span>)</a> sets the Union-wide performance targets, including a cost-efficiency target for <span class="oj-italic">en route</span> air navigation services expressed in determined unit costs for the provision of those services, for the second reference period, which covers the years 2015 to 2019 inclusive.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_3">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(3)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">Pursuant to Article 17(1)(b) and (c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, the Commission is to assess the unit rates for charging zones for 2015 submitted by the Member States to the Commission by 1 June 2014 following the requirements of Article 9(1) and 9(2) of that Regulation. That assessment concerns the compliance of those unit rates with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_4">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(4)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">The Commission has carried out its assessment of the unit rates with the support of the Performance Review Body, which is charged with assisting the Commission in the implementation of the performance scheme pursuant to Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 390/2013, and Eurocontrol's Central Route Charges Office, using the data and additional information provided by the Member States by 1 June 2014 as well as relevant information submitted as part of the performance plans. The assessment also took into account the explanations given and corrections made before the consultation meeting on the unit rates for 2015 for <span class="oj-italic">en route</span> services that was held on 25 and 26 June 2014 in application of Article 9(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, as well as the corrections by Member States to the unit rates following subsequent contacts between the Commission, the Performance Review Body and the Member States concerned. Furthermore, the assessment of the unit rates for 2015 has been based on the report by the PRB on the performance plans for the second reference period, which was submitted to the Commission on 7 October 2014 and subsequently updated on 15 December 2014.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_5">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(5)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">On the basis of that assessment, the Commission has found, in accordance with Article 17(1)(d) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, that the unit rates for charging zones for 2015 submitted by the United Kingdom, Ireland, Bulgaria, Romania, Cyprus, Greece, Malta, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Slovenia, Hungary, Poland, Lithuania, Denmark, Sweden, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Portugal and Spain are in compliance with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_6">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(6)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">Pursuant to Article 17(1)(d) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, the Member States concerned should be notified of that finding.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_7">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(7)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">The finding and notification that unit rates for charging zones are in compliance with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013 is without prejudice to Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 550/2004.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_8">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(8)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">Given that the final performance plans for the second reference period were not adopted before 1 November 2014, it is recalled that, in accordance with Article 17(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013, the Member States are required to recalculate the unit rates for charging zones for 2015 where necessary on the basis of the final adopted performance plans and apply those recalculated rates as early as possible in the course of 2015 and to carry over any difference due to the temporary application of the unit rates set out in this Decision in the calculation of the unit rates for 2016.</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="rct_9">
            <table width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0">
               <col width="4%"/>
               <col width="96%"/>
               <tbody>
                  <tr>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">(9)</p>
                     </td>
                     <td valign="top">
                        <p class="oj-normal">The Single Sky Committee did not deliver an opinion. An implementing act was deemed to be necessary and the chair submitted the draft implementing act to the appeal committee for further deliberation. The measures provided for in this Decision are in accordance with the opinion of the appeal committee,</p>
                     </td>
                  </tr>
               </tbody>
            </table>
         </div>
         <p class="oj-normal">HAS ADOPTED THIS DECISION:</p>
      </div>
      <div class="eli-subdivision" id="enc_1">
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="art_1">
            <p id="d1e205-25-1" class="oj-ti-art">Article 1</p>
            <p class="oj-normal">The unit rates for charging zones for 2015 set out in the Annex are in compliance with Implementing Regulations (EU) No 390/2013 and (EU) No 391/2013.</p>
         </div>
         <div class="eli-subdivision" id="art_2">
            <p id="d1e210-25-1" class="oj-ti-art">Article 2</p>
            <p class="oj-normal">This Decision is addressed to the Republic of Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, the Kingdom of Denmark, the Republic of Estonia, Ireland, the Hellenic Republic, the Kingdom of Spain, the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Cyprus, the Republic of Latvia, the Republic of Lithuania, Hungary, the Republic of Malta, the Republic of Poland, the Portuguese Republic, Romania, the Republic of Slovenia, the Republic of Finland, the Kingdom of Sweden and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.</p>
         </div>
      </div>
      <div class="eli-subdivision" id="fnp_1">
         <div class="oj-final">
            <p class="oj-normal">Done at Brussels, 27 April 2015.</p>
            <div class="oj-signatory">
               <p class="oj-signatory">
                  <span class="oj-italic">For the Commission</span>
               </p>
               <p class="oj-signatory">Violeta BULC
            </p>
               <p class="oj-signatory">
                  <span class="oj-italic">Member of the Commission</span>
               </p>
            </div>
         </div>
      </div>
      <hr class="oj-note"/>
      <p class="oj-note">
         <a id="ntr1-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0001" href="#ntc1-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0001">(<span class="oj-super">1</span>)</a>  
            <a href="./../../../legal-content/EN/AUTO/?uri=OJ:L:2004:096:TOC">OJ L 96, 31.3.2004, p. 10</a>.</p>
      <p class="oj-note">
         <a id="ntr2-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0002" href="#ntc2-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0002">(<span class="oj-super">2</span>)</a>  Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 391/2013 of 3 May 2013 laying down a common charging scheme for air navigation services (<a href="./../../../legal-content/EN/AUTO/?uri=OJ:L:2013:128:TOC">OJ L 128, 9.5.2013, p. 31</a>).</p>
      <p class="oj-note">
         <a id="ntr3-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0003" href="#ntc3-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0003">(<span class="oj-super">3</span>)</a>  Regulation (EC) No 549/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 March 2004 laying down the framework for the creation of the single European sky (the framework Regulation) (<a href="./../../../legal-content/EN/AUTO/?uri=OJ:L:2004:196:TOC">OJ L 196, 31.3.2004, p. 1</a>).</p>
      <p class="oj-note">
         <a id="ntr4-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0004" href="#ntc4-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0004">(<span class="oj-super">4</span>)</a>  Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 390/2013 of 3 May 2013 laying down a performance scheme for air navigation services and network functions (<a href="./../../../legal-content/EN/AUTO/?uri=OJ:L:2013:128:TOC">OJ L 128, 9.5.2013, p. 1</a>).</p>
      <p class="oj-note">
         <a id="ntr5-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0005" href="#ntc5-L_2015110EN.01002501-E0005">(<span class="oj-super">5</span>)</a>  Commission Implementing Decision 2014/132/EU of 11 March 2014 setting the Union-wide performance targets for the air traffic management network and alert thresholds for the second reference period 2015-19 (<a href="./../../../legal-content/EN/AUTO/?uri=OJ:L:2014:071:TOC">OJ L 71, 12.3.2014, p. 20</a>).</p>
   </div>
